title: Managing Property in India While Living Abroad: What an NRI Landlord Actually Needs in Place
subtitle: Leases, caretakers, property tax, society transfers, insurance and the paper trail that protects an owner who cannot visit
meta_description: What an NRI owner needs for letting, caretakers, tax, society transfers, insurance and encroachment risk on Indian property managed from abroad.
author: Bhaskar Subramanian
standfirst: An NRI who owns a flat, a house or a plot in India but lives abroad faces a problem resident owners rarely think about: almost every step in managing that property, letting it, collecting rent, paying tax, renewing a society membership, defending it against an encroacher, assumes an owner who can walk into an office, sign in person and turn up if something goes wrong. None of that changes because the owner happens to live in Dubai, London or Toronto. What changes is how the owner does it, and the gap between doing it properly and doing it loosely is usually invisible until a tenant stops paying, a society refuses to update its records, or a relative who was allowed to stay starts to act like an owner.
key_points: A lease exceeding one year, or reserving a yearly rent, must be registered under Section 17 of the Registration Act, 1908; this is why most residential lettings are kept to eleven months, but an unregistered document for a longer term cannot be used to prove the lease in court under Section 49 of the same Act.

The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 is a model law circulated to States for adaptation, not a central statute in force across India; adoption has been patchy and some of the figures reported for which States have adopted it conflict with each other, so the rent law actually governing a tenancy still has to be checked State by State.

Delhi's rent control law and West Bengal's Premises Tenancy Act, 1997 both let an owner recover possession on a bona fide personal-occupation ground, and Delhi High Court authority holds that an owner's NRI status or overseas residence does not by itself defeat that claim, though the owner still has to show a genuine, provable need.

A power of attorney signed outside India for use on Indian property is generally expected to carry attestation by the Indian embassy or consulate, or an apostille where the country is party to the Hague Convention, before it will be accepted for stamping and use at the Sub-Registrar's office in India; practice varies by registrar and this is best confirmed before the document is executed.

Mutation of a property in municipal or revenue records is an administrative, fiscal exercise; the Supreme Court has repeatedly held that a mutation entry does not by itself create, extinguish or prove title, so an NRI owner should not treat an updated mutation record as a substitute for the registered deed.

Tenant verification obligations are not uniform across India; Delhi Police material describes a duty on the owner to inform the local police of a new tenant, while the position in cities such as Mumbai is less settled in public guidance, so an owner managing a let property from abroad should check the current local police requirement rather than assume one national rule applies everywhere.

Recovering possession from an encroacher is a race against the Limitation Act, 1963; a suit based on title must ordinarily be filed within twelve years, and the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling in Ravinder Kaur Grewal v Manjit Kaur confirms that mere long possession, without an overt act asserting ownership, does not by itself amount to adverse possession against the true owner.

sections.heading: Why distance changes the practical risk, not the legal rule
paragraphs: Every legal obligation that attaches to owning property in India attaches equally to an owner who lives in Chennai and an owner who lives in Chicago. The lease still has to be registered on the same terms, the property tax still falls due on the same dates, the society's bye-laws still apply in the same way, and an encroacher's twelve-year clock under the Limitation Act, 1963 keeps running whether or not the owner is in the country to notice it. What distance actually changes is the owner's practical ability to catch a problem early and correct it cheaply.

A resident owner who notices a tenant falling behind on rent can usually resolve it, formally or informally, within weeks. An NRI owner often finds out only when the arrears have grown large enough that a relative or a caretaker finally sends word, or when a buyer's lawyer flags an unresolved tenancy during a title search years later. The same gap applies to a relative occupying a flat rent-free, to a society that has quietly stopped sending notices to an address nobody checks, and to a boundary wall that has crept a few feet over successive years of construction next door.

None of this calls for a different set of laws. It calls for the same documents, the same registrations and the same periodic checks that a careful resident owner would keep, done with more discipline because there is no opportunity to fix a gap by simply walking over and looking at the property. The sections that follow work through the main points where an NRI owner, managing property from abroad, needs to get the paperwork right the first time: letting the property, dealing with the tenant if things go wrong, appointing someone to act locally, keeping tax and society records current, insuring the property, and protecting it against encroachment.

sections.heading: Letting the property: registration, and why most leases are kept to eleven months
paragraphs: Section 17(1)(d) of the Registration Act, 1908, read with Section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, makes registration compulsory for a lease of immovable property from year to year, for any term exceeding one year, or reserving a yearly rent. Section 18 makes registration optional for a lease not exceeding one year. This is the entire reason the standard residential rent agreement in India runs for eleven months: it sits just under the compulsory-registration threshold, so the parties avoid stamp duty and registration fees that scale with the rent and the term.

The consequence of skipping registration on a lease that should have been registered is not a fine. It is evidentiary. Section 49 of the Registration Act says that a document required to be registered, if left unregistered, cannot be received as evidence of the transaction it records, and cannot be relied on to affect the immovable property. A landlord who wants to enforce an agreement running longer than a year, for instance to claim escalated rent under a clause that was never put into a registered document, may find the clause simply unusable in court. An eleven-month lease that is renewed informally, letter after letter, year after year, without ever being registered carries no similar problem, because each term individually falls under the optional-registration threshold.

A separate point that an owner letting property from abroad should check locally is that some States now require registration at a lower threshold than the national default. Uttar Pradesh, for example, has moved toward a tenancy law requiring registration of agreements running beyond eleven months on terms distinct from the general Registration Act position, and Maharashtra's own leave-and-licence practice has long treated registration of even short-term agreements as compulsory under State amendment, with the licensor bearing responsibility for getting it done. None of this is uniform, and an owner should confirm the current registration rule for the State where the property actually sits rather than assume the eleven-month convention is a safe default everywhere.

A written, signed, dated lease, registered where the law requires it and kept on file in both physical and scanned form, remains the single most useful document an NRI landlord can hold. It fixes the rent, the term, the security deposit, maintenance responsibility and the notice period in a form that survives disputes about memory or intention far better than an oral understanding conveyed through a relative.

sections.heading: Which rent law actually governs the tenancy
paragraphs: A common misconception among owners living abroad is that a single, modern national rent law now covers the whole country. It does not. The Union Cabinet approved the Model Tenancy Act in 2021 and circulated it to States and Union Territories as a model for them to adopt or adapt; it was never enacted as a central law binding every State on its own force. Adoption since then has been limited and the public record on exactly which States have adopted it is inconsistent between sources, so an owner cannot assume the Model Tenancy Act's provisions, including its rent authority and rent court structure, govern a tenancy simply because the Act exists.

What this means in practice is that the rent law actually governing a given tenancy depends on where the property is. Delhi tenancies above a certain threshold fall outside the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 and are governed instead by ordinary civil law and the Transfer of Property Act. Delhi tenancies within the Act's coverage go through the Rent Controller. West Bengal tenancies are governed by the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997, which has its own eviction grounds, notice requirements and forum, the Civil Judge exercising powers under the Act, distinct from an ordinary title suit. Maharashtra has its own rent legislation, and several States that have genuinely adopted Model Tenancy Act-style reforms have set up a separate Rent Authority and Rent Court structure that has no equivalent where the older rent control statute still applies.

For an NRI landlord, the practical step is not to research every State's rent law in the abstract but to confirm, for the specific property, which statute applies, what notice the owner must give before filing for possession, and which forum hears the case. That single piece of information shapes every later decision about how to draft the lease and how to respond if the tenant stops paying or refuses to leave.

sections.heading: Recovering the property if the tenant will not leave
paragraphs: Where a State rent control statute applies, the grounds for evicting a tenant are usually limited to the grounds the statute lists, and personal, bona fide requirement of the premises by the owner is one of the most commonly used. Section 14(1)(e) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 lets the Rent Controller order eviction where the landlord genuinely needs the premises for personal occupation and has no other reasonably suitable accommodation, and such petitions can follow the summary procedure under Section 25B rather than a full trial. Section 9 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997 similarly lists the landlord's requirement of the premises for personal occupation as a ground, subject to a notice period before a suit for recovery on that ground can be filed, and the tenant remains a protected statutory tenant until a decree for eviction actually follows.

An NRI owner understandably worries that overseas residence will be used against this claim, on the theory that someone who lives abroad cannot genuinely need to occupy a Delhi or Kolkata flat. Delhi High Court authority has gone the other way. A 2025 ruling held that a landlord's residence abroad, NRI status or financial position does not by itself defeat a bona fide requirement claim, and that the landlord is not required to prove destitution or a permanent, immediate return to India to succeed on the ground. Earlier authority has treated even a need for frequent visits and temporary stays during those visits as sufficient to found the claim. None of this means every NRI landlord automatically wins; the tenant can still contest whether the stated need is genuine, and the landlord still has to show a credible, specific case rather than a bare assertion.

Outside rent control, where the tenancy is not covered by a State statute or the premises fall above whatever exemption threshold the statute sets, the route is an ordinary civil suit for eviction and recovery of possession under the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, generally preceded by a notice to quit under Section 106 of that Act. This route takes longer than a summary rent-control petition but is not confined to the limited statutory grounds, so a landlord with a lease that has simply expired, or a tenant holding over without any claim to a fresh term, can use it even without showing bona fide personal need.

An owner managing this from abroad should expect to act through a power of attorney holder or a local lawyer for every procedural step, filing, appearing through counsel, collecting process, while reserving the owner's own evidence, where the facts genuinely require the owner's personal knowledge, for recording by video conference through a court-appointed commission rather than delegating that evidence to the attorney. An attorney can act for the owner; an attorney cannot usually give evidence of facts that are within the owner's own knowledge and not the attorney's.

sections.heading: The power of attorney: getting the execution right the first time
paragraphs: Almost everything described in this article, signing a fresh lease, filing an eviction petition, attending a mutation hearing, executing a society transfer form, depends on the owner having a valid power of attorney in the hands of someone who can act locally. The mechanics of executing, attesting and registering that document, and the specific risks of relying on a general power of attorney for a property transaction, are substantial enough to warrant separate treatment, and this firm's article on using a power of attorney from abroad for Indian property and court matters covers that ground in detail.

The point worth flagging here, because it affects every transaction described in the rest of this article, is that a power of attorney signed outside India is commonly expected, by Sub-Registrars and by banks, to carry either attestation by the Indian embassy or consulate in the country where it was signed, or an apostille where that country is party to the Hague Apostille Convention, before it is accepted for stamping and use in India. Practice on exactly how strictly this is enforced varies between registration offices, and an owner should confirm the current requirement with the specific Sub-Registrar's office, or with counsel familiar with that office's practice, before executing the document rather than after. A power of attorney executed on plain paper abroad does not need an Indian stamp paper at the point of signing; stamping and adjudication, where required, generally happen after the document reaches India.

A power of attorney is also not permanent by default. It should state whether it is general or limited to specific acts, name the attorney precisely, and record, if the owner intends this, that it survives until expressly revoked. An owner who changes the person acting locally, for whatever reason, needs to revoke the earlier power of attorney in a form the relevant registrar and any bank or society will recognise, not simply stop using it, because an unrevoked power of attorney remains legally capable of being used by the person named in it.

sections.heading: Caretakers, property managers, and the line between a licence and a tenancy
paragraphs: Many NRI owners leave a relative, a former employee, or a professional property manager in charge of an empty or partly let property, with permission to stay on the premises in exchange for looking after it. This arrangement is ordinarily a licence, a personal permission to occupy that creates no interest in the property, and under Section 60 of the Indian Easements Act, 1882 a licence of this kind is generally revocable at the will of the owner, subject to limited exceptions, for instance where the licensee has, with the owner's consent and at the licensee's own expense, executed a work of a permanent character on the property in reliance on the licence.

The risk an owner managing this from abroad should watch for is drift: a caretaker who was meant to occupy a single room ends up occupying the whole property; a property manager who was meant to collect rent and remit it starts paying society charges and utility bills in their own name; a relative who was asked to keep an eye on the flat begins treating correspondence addressed to the flat as their own. None of this, by itself, converts a licence into a tenancy or starts an adverse possession clock, but it makes the facts harder to prove later if the arrangement ever needs to be terminated and the occupant resists. A short, dated letter recording that the occupation is a revocable licence, not a tenancy, and specifying what the caretaker is and is not permitted to do, costs little and is worth far more than its length suggests if the relationship later turns adversarial.

Separately, an owner who does let the property to a paying tenant should be aware that several cities treat informing the local police of a new tenant as an obligation on the owner, not merely a courtesy. Delhi Police material describes this as a requirement on the house owner whenever a tenant is taken in. The position elsewhere is less consistent in public guidance; Mumbai's tenant information process, for instance, has been described in different sources as both a formal requirement and as something short of a strict permit, and the practical enforcement differs by city and by local police station. An owner should check the current requirement for the specific city before letting the property, both because non-compliance can carry its own consequences and because the verification record itself is useful evidence of who was in occupation and from when.

sections.heading: Property tax, mutation, and why an updated record is not the same as proof of title
paragraphs: Property tax remains payable to the municipal or panchayat authority regardless of where the owner lives, and an owner who lets the arrears accumulate while abroad exposes the property to recovery proceedings and interest that are far easier to deal with when caught early. Arranging for the tax to be paid each year, whether through a local attorney, a property manager, or increasingly through a municipality's own online payment portal, is one of the simplest risk-reduction steps available and one of the easiest to neglect precisely because nothing visibly goes wrong for a long time after a payment is missed.

Mutation, the process of updating the owner's name in municipal or revenue records after a purchase, inheritance or transfer, is a different exercise from registration and should not be treated as a substitute for it. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that a mutation entry is made for fiscal purposes, to identify who should be assessed to pay land revenue or property tax, and does not by itself create, extinguish or conclusively prove title to the property. In Bhimabai Mahadeo Kambekar v Arthur Import and Export Company, the Court held in terms that mutation of land in revenue records neither creates nor extinguishes title, nor carries any presumptive value on title. The Court has also struck down an attempt by a State authority to make proof of mutation a precondition for registering a sale deed, on the footing that doing so would effectively convert a fiscal record into a title document, which the law does not permit.

For an NRI owner, the practical point is to keep mutation records updated, because banks and buyers do check them as part of ordinary diligence and an out-of-date record invites unnecessary questions, while understanding that an updated mutation entry is not itself proof of ownership and does not cure a defect in the underlying chain of registered title. If a dispute over ownership ever arises, the registered deed, the chain of earlier registered transfers, and any probate or succession document remain the documents that actually establish title; the mutation record is administrative support for that title, not a replacement for it.

sections.heading: Society share transfers, utility accounts, and keeping records in the owner's name
paragraphs: Where the property is a flat in a cooperative housing society or an apartment owned through a society or association, the society's own records, membership, the share certificate, the no-objection certificate on a transfer, matter in practice even though they do not themselves confer or defeat title. An NRI owner who inherits a flat, or who buys one from abroad through an attorney, should ensure the society's register is updated to reflect the new ownership and that the share certificate is transferred, because societies in practice rely on their own membership records when recognising who may vote, who may authorise alterations, and who the society will deal with on maintenance and redevelopment questions. The specific procedure, forms and any fee the society may charge are governed by the applicable State's cooperative societies legislation and the society's own bye-laws, which differ enough between States that an owner should confirm the current requirement with the society and, where a dispute arises over an unreasonable refusal to transfer, with counsel rather than assume a single national procedure applies.

The same discipline applies to utility connections, electricity, water, and piped gas where applicable. Keeping these in the owner's name, or formally transferred to a tenant's name under a documented arrangement that reverts on the tenant's exit, avoids a common problem where a long-staying occupant's name on a utility bill later gets cited, rightly or wrongly, as evidence of a tenancy or even of a possessory claim stronger than the occupant actually has. An owner letting the property should decide, and record in the lease, whether utility accounts move to the tenant's name for the term and are to be transferred back, or remain in the owner's name with the tenant simply paying the bills; either is workable, but leaving the question unaddressed invites exactly the kind of ambiguity that makes a later dispute harder to resolve.

sections.heading: Insurance for a let-out or vacant property
paragraphs: A property that is let to a tenant, occupied by a caretaker, or simply standing vacant for long stretches carries risks a resident owner would normally manage by being present, fire, water damage, theft, and structural damage from natural causes. An owner living abroad cannot rely on physical proximity to catch these early, which makes an appropriate property insurance policy, covering the structure and, where relevant, fixtures and contents, a more significant protection than it might be for a resident owner who visits the property regularly.

The specific terms, premium and exclusions available vary by insurer and by whether the property is occupied, let or vacant, and some policies treat extended vacancy as a condition requiring separate disclosure or carrying different terms. Rather than assume a standard homeowner's policy covers a property let to a tenant on the same terms as an owner-occupied property, an NRI owner should check the policy wording for how it treats tenancy and vacancy before relying on it, and should keep the policy, the premium receipts and a record of what the policy actually covers among the documents a local attorney or property manager can access if a claim ever needs to be made while the owner is not in the country.

sections.heading: Encroachment, and the limitation clock that keeps running while the owner is away
paragraphs: An owner living abroad is, in practical terms, more exposed to encroachment than a resident owner, simply because physical absence makes it harder to notice a boundary wall that has shifted, a shed that has appeared on vacant land, or a tenant whose possession has outlasted any claim of right and who now resists leaving. The legal rules that apply to this situation are detailed in this firm's article on remedies when a relative, tenant or encroacher occupies an NRI's property, and are not repeated at length here. What matters for an owner managing property from abroad is the limitation point that sits underneath every one of those remedies.

Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 gives twelve years, running from the date possession becomes adverse to the true owner, for a suit to recover possession of immovable property based on title; the period runs to thirty years where the property belongs to the government. The Supreme Court's 2019 decision in Ravinder Kaur Grewal v Manjit Kaur confirmed that a person who has genuinely perfected title through adverse possession may rely on that title offensively, as a plaintiff, and not merely defensively against a suit brought by the original owner. The same line of authority is equally clear that mere long, continuous possession is not, by itself, adverse possession; the occupant's possession must be hostile to the true owner's title, open, and continuous for the statutory period, with some overt act asserting ownership inconsistent with the true owner's title, for the clock to run in the occupant's favour at all.

The practical consequence for an owner abroad is that the time to notice an encroachment or an occupant who is overstaying a licence or a tenancy is well before the twelve-year period runs its course, not after. A periodic visit, a trusted local contact who checks the property and reports back, dated photographs, and prompt written objection the moment an occupant's conduct looks like an assertion of ownership rather than permitted use, are all steps that cost little and that materially strengthen an owner's later position if a dispute does arise. Waiting to act until a title search for a sale reveals a problem that has been developing for a decade is the single most expensive way to discover one.

sections.heading: The documents an NRI landlord should hold, and where each one earns its place
paragraphs: No single document protects an owner managing property from abroad. What protects the owner is a set of documents, kept current and accessible to whoever acts locally, each doing a distinct job. The registered sale deed and the earlier chain of title remain the foundation; nothing else in this list substitutes for them. A current encumbrance certificate, obtained from the Sub-Registrar's office, shows whether any mortgage, charge or pending litigation has been registered against the property and should be refreshed before any sale, mortgage or major transaction, not relied on indefinitely from an old copy.

The lease itself, registered where the law requires registration, with rent receipts or bank transfer records that independently corroborate the tenancy, protects the owner's ability to prove both the terms of the letting and that rent was actually paid, which matters for tax purposes as much as for any later dispute. Proof of tenant verification, where the local police require it, both satisfies that local obligation and creates an independent record of who was in occupation and from when. The power of attorney, properly attested and, where the transaction requires it, registered, is what makes every other document usable by someone acting on the owner's behalf; without a valid, current power of attorney in the right hands, none of the rest can be acted upon quickly from abroad.

Property tax receipts and an updated mutation extract support the owner's position in dealings with the municipality and with buyers or lenders carrying out diligence, even though, as explained above, they do not themselves prove title. The society share certificate and transfer records matter wherever the property sits within a housing society. The insurance policy and premium receipts matter if anything goes wrong physically to the structure. And a simple, maintained file of correspondence, letters to tenants, caretakers or occupants recording the terms on which they hold the property, dated photographs of the property's condition and boundaries taken periodically, and a note of who has visited and when, often turns out, in a dispute years later, to be the difference between a claim that can be proved quickly and one that cannot be proved at all.

sections.heading: Keeping oversight without being present
paragraphs: A property managed well from abroad is usually not one with the most elaborate paperwork; it is one with the simplest, most repeatable routine for checking on it. A single trusted local point of contact, whether a family member, a professional property manager or the same local attorney who holds the power of attorney, who visits periodically, photographs the property's condition and boundaries, and reports back on anything unusual, does more to prevent disputes than any document drafted after a problem has already started. Where no family member is available or willing, paid property management services exist precisely to fill this gap, and their fee is ordinarily far smaller than the cost of litigating a dispute that could have been caught early.

Rent collected on a let property, where the owner is an NRI, is usually credited to a Non-Resident Ordinary account rather than a Non-Resident External account, since rental income earned in India is current income arising from an Indian source and is treated differently under foreign exchange rules from funds an NRI brings in from abroad. The mechanics of NRE, NRO and FCNR accounts, and what can and cannot be repatriated from each, are covered in detail in this firm's article on those accounts under FEMA and are not repeated here; the point relevant to property management is simply that rent should be collected into the correct account from the outset, rather than mixed with other funds, so that tax withholding and any later repatriation are straightforward to document.

Finally, an owner should periodically review who currently holds a valid power of attorney, confirm that contact details for the local attorney, the property manager and the society are current, and keep copies of every document described in this article, the lease, the encumbrance certificate, tax receipts, the mutation extract, the insurance policy and the power of attorney itself, somewhere the owner can reach quickly from abroad, rather than only in a drawer inside the property itself. A file that takes an afternoon to assemble once saves weeks of delay if a dispute, a sale, or an inheritance ever requires producing these documents on short notice.

conclusion: None of the obligations described in this article are unusual or especially burdensome taken one at a time. Register the lease where the law requires it. Confirm which rent statute actually governs the tenancy before assuming a national model law applies. Get the power of attorney attested correctly the first time. Keep property tax and mutation current without mistaking either for proof of title. Insure the property on terms that actually match how it is occupied. And treat the twelve-year limitation clock on adverse possession as something to act on early, not something to discover has already run.

The difficulty for an owner abroad is not any one of these steps; it is that neglecting several of them at once, over years of distance and reliance on informal family or neighbourly goodwill, tends to surface all together, usually at the worst possible moment, a sale falling through, a tenant refusing to leave, or a relative's long occupation hardening into a claim the owner never anticipated having to answer. Building the habit of keeping these documents current, and having a local attorney who can act on short notice under a valid power of attorney, converts most of these risks from emergencies into routine administration.

faqs.q: Can I let out my flat in India on an informal, unregistered agreement if I trust the tenant?
faqs.a: You can, and for a term of eleven months or less this is legally common and the agreement remains usable as evidence. The risk appears only if the arrangement runs longer than a year or reserves a yearly rent, since Section 17 of the Registration Act then makes registration compulsory, and an unregistered document for such a term cannot be used as evidence of the transaction under Section 49. Keep the agreement written and dated even for a short term, and register it where the term or the State's own rules require it.

faqs.q: I live in Dubai. Will a court assume I cannot really need my Kolkata or Delhi flat for personal use?
faqs.a: Not on that basis alone. Delhi High Court authority has specifically held that NRI status and overseas residence do not by themselves defeat a bona fide personal-requirement claim, and that the owner need not prove an immediate, permanent return to India. You still have to show a genuine, specific need, visits, a planned return, a family member's use, rather than a bare assertion, and the tenant can contest whether that need is real.

faqs.q: Does the Model Tenancy Act apply to my tenancy automatically now that it has been approved by the Union Cabinet?
faqs.a: No. The Model Tenancy Act, 2021 was circulated to States as a model for them to adopt, amend or ignore; it is not itself a central law in force nationwide. Which rent law actually governs your tenancy depends on whether, and in what form, the State where the property sits has legislated along these lines, and the public record on which States have done so is not entirely consistent, so this should be confirmed for the specific property rather than assumed.

faqs.q: My power of attorney was notarised in the country where I live. Is that enough to use it in India?
faqs.a: Often not by itself. Sub-Registrars and banks in India commonly expect a power of attorney executed abroad to carry attestation by the Indian embassy or consulate in that country, or an apostille where the country is party to the Hague Apostille Convention, before accepting it for stamping and use. Practice differs between registration offices, so confirm the specific requirement with the Sub-Registrar's office that will handle the transaction before the document is executed, not after.

faqs.q: My caretaker has lived in my flat for ten years looking after it. Could this turn into a claim against my ownership?
faqs.a: A caretaker's occupation under your permission is ordinarily a revocable licence under Section 60 of the Indian Easements Act, and long occupation under permission does not by itself become adverse possession; adverse possession requires the occupant's conduct to become hostile to your title, openly and to your knowledge, for the statutory period to start running against you. It is still good practice to record the arrangement in a dated letter describing it as a licence, precisely so that there is no ambiguity if the relationship ever turns adversarial.

faqs.q: Is an updated mutation record in my name enough to prove I own the property?
faqs.a: No. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that mutation entries are made for fiscal and administrative purposes and do not by themselves create, extinguish or conclusively prove title. Keep the mutation record current because municipalities, banks and buyers rely on it in practice, but the registered deed and the chain of title behind it remain the documents that actually establish ownership.

faqs.q: How long does an encroacher need to be in possession before they can claim my land?
faqs.a: Twelve years from the date possession became adverse to you, under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963, for privately owned land, and thirty years where the land belongs to the government. The twelve years runs from when the occupant's possession turned hostile and open, not necessarily from when they first entered, and mere long possession without an overt act asserting ownership does not start this clock at all. The safer course is to act on any encroachment, or any occupant who seems to be asserting ownership, as soon as you become aware of it rather than waiting to see how long it has been going on.

faqs.q: Do I need to insure a flat that is standing empty between tenants?
faqs.a: It is generally advisable, and worth checking before assuming your existing policy covers it. Many property insurance policies treat extended vacancy differently from an occupied or let property, sometimes requiring separate disclosure or carrying different terms, so confirm the policy wording for how it treats a vacant period rather than assuming continuous cover.

verification_notes: Section 17(1)(d) and Section 18, Registration Act, 1908, on the compulsory and optional registration thresholds for leases, and Section 49 on the evidentiary consequence of non-registration: confirmed from a reproduction of the Act's provisions, a Supreme Court-referenced Orissa High Court PDF on the 11-month exemption, and independent secondary explainer sources (lawtrend.in, outlookmoney.com) describing the same threshold; consistent across sources.

Model Tenancy Act, 2021 status as a model law circulated for State adaptation rather than a binding central statute: confirmed from multiple sources, but the specific list of States reported to have adopted it conflicted between a Rajya Sabha reply described in one source (naming Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Andaman and Nicobar, Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu, and Lakshadweep) and an older report naming a different set of four States; this article states only the uncontested point, that adoption is State-specific and limited, and does not assert a specific current list of adopting States.

Section 14(1)(e) and Section 25B, Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 on bona fide personal requirement and the summary procedure: confirmed from a Mondaq legal commentary and corroborated by case-law references on Indian Kanoon's future document viewer; the 2025 Delhi High Court ruling on NRI status not defeating a bona fide claim is reported in a single dedicated news source (lawyerenews.com) with matching detail recounted in the Mondaq commentary's general discussion of the bona fide requirement doctrine, so it is described in this article without an exact case citation.

Section 9, West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997 on the own-occupation eviction ground, and Section 6 on the pre-suit notice period: confirmed from the Act's text as hosted on indiacode.nic.in and corroborated by case-law discussion of the statutory tenancy created under the Act found via Indian Kanoon's future document viewer.

Ravinder Kaur Grewal v Manjit Kaur, (2019) 8 SCC 729, and its holding that a plaintiff may sue on title perfected by adverse possession, together with the requirement that mere long possession without an overt hostile act is not adverse possession: confirmed from the official Supreme Court judgment PDF hosted on digiscr.sci.gov.in, and corroborated by SCC Online's and LiveLaw's independent summaries of the same ruling.

Article 65, Limitation Act, 1963, twelve years for private immovable property and thirty years for government land, running from when possession becomes adverse: confirmed from the Ravinder Kaur Grewal judgment itself and from independent secondary commentary (bhattandjoshiassociates.com) describing the same distinction between private and government land.

Bhimabai Mahadeo Kambekar v Arthur Import and Export Company on mutation entries not creating or extinguishing title, and the related Samiullah line of authority on mutation not being a precondition for registration of a sale deed: confirmed from the Supreme Court's own judgment PDF (api.sci.gov.in) referenced in search results and corroborated independently by LiveLaw's and SCC Online's summaries of the same and related rulings; this article states the settled principle and does not rely on any single secondary source alone for it.

Power of attorney executed abroad requiring Indian consular attestation or an apostille before use at an Indian Sub-Registrar's office: confirmed from two independent law-firm sources (advocategandhi.com and nriinformation.com) describing the same practical requirement; both sources note that practice and strictness vary by registrar, and this article reflects that qualification rather than stating the requirement as a uniform, invariable rule across India.

Section 60, Indian Easements Act, 1882 on the revocability of a licence and the permanent-structure exception: confirmed from case-law summaries referenced via Legitquest and Casemine search results describing the same statutory text and exception; specific case names behind those summaries were not retained as precise, checkable citations in this research round and are therefore not attributed to a named judgment in the article text.

Tenant police verification as an owner obligation in Delhi, and the inconsistent public description of the position in Mumbai: confirmed from Delhi Police-referenced guidance summarised by multiple secondary sources (nobroker.in, rentok.com, housing.com) and from conflicting secondary accounts of Mumbai's tenant information process; because the sources genuinely conflict on Mumbai, this article states that the position is less settled in public guidance there rather than asserting a specific rule.

Left out or stated only in general terms: specific figures for fines under any State Police Act for failing to carry out tenant verification were reported in only a single secondary source and are not repeated here; a reported Karnataka Rent Act amendment said to take effect in January 2026 was found in only one secondary blog and could not be independently corroborated, so it is omitted; this article does not list which States besides Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra have altered the standard Registration Act thresholds for leases, since no comprehensive, current State-by-State source was found, and readers are directed to confirm the position for the specific State rather than being given an unverified list.
